scenarios.title: Ransomware
scenarios.blurb: Files are being encrypted across the business. Contain it, keep people informed and get running again.

recap.text: The attack hit **{sys}**.
The backups were **clean**.
The backups were **encrypted too**.
Customer data **was stolen**.
Customer data **wasn’t taken**.

text: Morning. Antivirus on {count} {team} laptops has flagged files being renamed to {ext} in the last ten minutes. One of them is still doing it.
Heads up: {count} laptops in {team} are renaming their files to {ext}. Antivirus caught it about ten minutes ago and one is still going.
We’ve got a problem. Files on {count} {team} laptops are turning into {ext} files, and it’s still happening on one of them.

options.text: Isolate those {count} laptops from the network
options.note: Fast, targeted containment of the machines you know about.

reply.text: Done, they’re cut off. Checking everything else now.

options.text: Shut down the whole network now
options.note: It stops the spread, but it stops the whole business too. Heavy-handed for a few laptops.

reply.text: Everything’s down. The phones are ringing off the hook.

options.text: Email all staff telling them to switch off their computers
options.note: Slow and patchy, and email might not be trustworthy during an attack. Isolate the known machines first.

reply.text: Some people have switched off. Two laptops are still encrypting.

options.text: Keep watching to learn more first
options.note: Ransomware encrypts more with every minute it runs. Contain first, investigate after.

reply.text: Two more laptops have just started renaming files.

text: Bad news: it’s on {sys} too. I’ve got two people free right now.
It’s spread to {sys}. I can spare two people, no more.
{Sys} is showing the same file names. Two of my team are free.

options.text: Disconnect {sys} from the network
options.note: Cutting off the biggest infected system limits how far it spreads.

options.text: Reset admin passwords and disable the accounts being used
options.note: Attackers usually move around with stolen admin accounts. Taking them away slows them down.

options.text: Take disk and memory images before anything is wiped
options.note: Evidence now is what lets you find out how they got in tomorrow.

options.text: Wipe and rebuild the infected laptops straight away
options.note: Gets people working sooner, but destroys the evidence of how the attackers got in.

text: There’s a note on the screens demanding {ransom} in bitcoin within {deadline}. Can we just pay and make this go away?
They want {ransom} in bitcoin, deadline {deadline}. Honestly, is paying the quickest way out?
A ransom note says {ransom} within {deadline} or they publish everything. Should we just pay it?

messages.text: We do have cyber insurance. I’m finding the policy now.

options.text: Don’t pay for now. Call the insurer’s incident line and report it to Action Fraud
options.note: Insurers provide specialist responders, and reporting gets you help. Paying funds crime and doesn’t guarantee your data back.

reply.text: The insurer’s team will join a call at 11. They said not to contact the attackers.

options.text: Pay quickly to limit the damage
options.note: There’s no guarantee of a working key, you mark yourselves as a payer, and it could breach sanctions law.

reply.text: I don’t even know how to buy bitcoin. This could take days.

options.text: Contact the attackers ourselves to buy time
options.note: Any contact should go through specialists your insurer provides. Amateur negotiation can make things worse.

reply.text: They replied straight away. Now they say the deadline is 24 hours.

options.text: Leave it to Dana
options.note: Without your advice, the CEO is left to make a high-stakes decision alone.

reply.text: I’ll wait to hear from you, but not for long.

text: Staff are asking on WhatsApp what’s going on, and a customer has posted that our website’s down.
People are starting to talk. Two customers have posted that they can’t reach us.
The switchboard is getting calls about the outage, and staff are asking me what to say.

options.text: A short, honest holding statement: we’re dealing with a cyber incident, some services are down, next update at 3pm
options.note: Brief, honest and with a time for the next update. It steadies people without guessing at details.

reply.text: Out now. The replies are mostly supportive.

options.text: Say nothing until we know everything
options.note: Silence gets filled by rumour. You can say a little without knowing everything.

reply.text: Someone’s posted that we’ve been hacked and are hiding it.

options.text: Say it’s planned maintenance
options.note: If it comes out later, and it usually does, trust drops much further than if you’d been honest.

reply.text: A member of staff has already replied saying it isn’t maintenance.

options.text: Publish the full technical details now
options.note: Too much detail too early can be wrong and can help the attackers. Keep it short until you know more.

reply.text: That post mentions the admin accounts we haven’t finished resetting.

messages.text: Reminder that Dana’s flown out to the Lisbon conference this afternoon.
New alert: Dana’s account has just signed in from Lisbon.

beats.ask: How do you handle the alert?

options.text: Check with Dana on her known mobile number before acting
options.note: It was really her. Checking first avoided cutting off your CEO in the middle of a crisis.

reply.text: Yes, that’s me, just landed. Thanks for checking.

options.text: Lock Dana’s account immediately
options.note: Cautious, but she was genuinely in Lisbon. A quick check on a known number would have avoided locking out the CEO.

reply.text: Dana’s locked out and can’t join the insurer’s call.

options.text: Ignore it, there’s too much going on
options.note: It was genuine this time, but during an attack ignored alerts are exactly where attackers hide.

reply.text: Logged it, but nobody’s checked it.

messages.text: The disk images show how they got in: a phishing email on Friday, then a stolen admin account. We know what to close.

outcomes.note: Because you kept evidence, the investigation found the way in.

messages.text: We can’t tell how they got in. The infected laptops were rebuilt, so the evidence is gone. They may still have a way back.

outcomes.note: Wiping before taking evidence meant the way in couldn’t be found.

messages.text: The logs point to a phishing email, but without disk images we can’t be certain.

outcomes.note: Without images, the investigation can only guess at the way in.

messages.text: Good news: last night’s backups are clean and were offline. We can restore {sys}.
Bad news: the backups on the network were encrypted too. The offline copy is a week old.

options.text: Rebuild it clean, then restore last night’s backup
options.note: Clean rebuild plus clean backups: the textbook recovery.

reply.text: Restoring now. Should be back by this evening.

options.text: Rebuild it clean, restore the week-old copy and re-enter the missing week
options.note: Slower and painful, but it gets you back on a system you can trust.

reply.text: It’ll be a long week, but we’ll get there.

options.text: Check No More Ransom for a free decryptor while rebuilding
options.note: Free decryptors exist for some ransomware families. Worth a check alongside rebuilding.

reply.text: No free decryptor for this one, but we’ve ruled it out. Rebuilding.

options.text: Bring it back online as it is, we need it today
options.note: Without a clean rebuild, anything the attackers left behind comes straight back with it.

reply.text: Alert: suspicious activity on {sys} again.

messages.text: Aisha’s confirmed that customer names, addresses and order histories were copied out before the encryption started. We became aware of that yesterday.

beats.ask: Do we report it to the ICO?

options.text: Yes, report now (within 72 hours) and add details as we learn them
options.note: UK GDPR requires a report within 72 hours of becoming aware. You can send it in stages.

reply.text: Submitted. I’ll send updates as the investigation goes on.

options.text: Wait until the investigation is finished
options.note: The 72 hours started when you became aware. Report what you know now and add the rest later.

reply.text: Okay, but the clock started yesterday.

options.text: Don’t report, it’s only names and addresses
options.note: Personal data was taken, so it’s reportable. Under-reporting is a breach of its own.

reply.text: I have to put on record that I disagree.

messages.text: Good news: no sign that any personal data left the network. It was encrypted, not copied.

beats.ask: What do we do about data protection?

options.text: Record the decision and our reasons in the breach log
options.note: Even when you don’t need to report, you must record the incident and why you decided not to.

reply.text: Logged, with the evidence attached.

options.text: Report it to the ICO anyway, just in case
options.note: Not required here, and not harmful, but recording your reasons is the key step.

reply.text: Sent. They may ask why we reported.

options.text: Nothing to record, no data was lost
options.note: Personal data was still unavailable for a while. Breaches must be recorded even if not reported.

reply.text: We should at least log it.

text: I’m writing about the outage at {org}. Was customer data stolen? My deadline is 5pm.
Hi, Northern Post here. We’ve heard {org} has been hit by ransomware. Can you confirm whether customer data was taken? We go to print at 5.
A source tells me {org} is about to pay the hackers. Was customer data stolen? I need a response by 5pm.

options.text: Give an agreed, honest statement, including what we’re doing for customers

variants.note: Honest and prepared, with customers already being contacted. The story is about how you handled it.
Honest and prepared. Saying what you know, and what you don’t, protects trust.

reply.text: Thanks, that’s helpful. I’ll include your statement in full.

options.text: No comment
options.note: ‘No comment’ reads as hiding something. A short agreed statement is better.

reply.text: I’ll say {org} declined to comment.

options.text: Say no customer data was taken

variants.note: True this time, but risky to state so firmly while the investigation is still going on.
It was, and you knew. Misleading the press turns an incident into a scandal.

reply.text: Noted. I’ll quote that.

messages.text: We’re back up and running. What’s the one thing we do first so this doesn’t happen again?

options.text: Hold a lessons-learned review and fix the top three gaps it finds
options.note: A blameless review turns this incident into specific fixes, and shows regulators you’ve learned.

reply.text: Book it for next week, everyone involved.

options.text: Turn on multi-factor sign-in everywhere, starting with admin accounts
options.note: The attackers used a stolen password. MFA would have stopped that step.

reply.text: Admins by Friday, everyone else this month.

options.text: Phishing training for all staff
options.note: Helpful, but people will always click sometimes. Pair it with technical controls like MFA.

reply.text: I’ll get it scheduled.

options.text: Buy a new antivirus product
options.note: The antivirus spotted it. The gaps were the stolen account and the response, not the tool.

reply.text: That’s a big spend. Are we sure it’s the problem?

messages.text: We reported to the ICO on day four, past the 72 hours. They’ve asked us to explain the delay.

outcomes.note: The ICO report went in after 72 hours.

messages.text: The decryption key we paid for only unlocked half the files, and now they’re asking for more.

outcomes.note: Paying didn’t bring everything back.

messages.text: {Sys} had to be taken down again overnight to clean it properly.

outcomes.note: Rushing the system back meant doing the work twice.

messages.text: Waiting at the start cost us five more laptops’ worth of files.

outcomes.note: The early wait let it spread further.

messages.text: Thank you, everyone. That was hard, and it was handled.

outcomes.note: The incident was closed without nasty surprises.

scenarios.title: Invoice fraud
scenarios.blurb: A supplier’s ‘new bank details’ arrive just before a big payment. Stop the money, find the hole, and keep everyone onside.

recap.text: The **{amount}** payment had **already gone** before anyone noticed.
The payment was **stopped** before it went out.
The attacker **was inside** your Accounts mailbox.
The emails came **from outside**; your mailboxes weren’t touched.

text: We paid {supplier}’s invoice of {amount} this morning, to the new bank details they emailed last week. They’ve just rung asking where their money is.
{Supplier} have called chasing {amount}. We paid it at 10 this morning, to the new account in their email. They say they never changed banks.
I was about to pay {supplier}’s invoice of {amount} to the new bank details they emailed last week. Something felt off, so I’ve paused it.
Before I send {amount} to {supplier}: their email says they’ve changed banks. It looks right, but I wanted to check with someone.

beats.ask: What’s the first thing you do?

options.text: Call our bank’s fraud team now to try to stop or recall the payment
options.note: Speed matters most. Banks can often freeze money in the first hours, but not after it’s moved on.

reply.text: Bank’s on it. They’ve flagged it with the receiving bank.

options.text: Keep it on hold and call {supplier} on the number we already have
options.note: A call-back on a number you already trust is the single best defence against invoice fraud.

reply.text: They’ve never changed banks. The email was fake. Payment stays on hold.

options.text: Reply to the email asking {supplier} to confirm the new details
options.note: If the email is fake or the thread is hijacked, you’re asking the attacker to confirm their own details.

reply.text: They replied in two minutes: ‘Yes, all correct, please proceed.’

options.text: Pay it. The email came from a real thread with them
options.note: Real threads get hijacked. New bank details always need a call-back, whatever the email looks like.

reply.text: Sent. I’ll let them know.

options.text: Leave it until tomorrow to see if it sorts itself out
options.note: Fraudsters move money within hours. Waiting until tomorrow usually means it’s gone.

reply.text: Okay, I’ll look again in the morning.

messages.text: The ‘new bank details’ email came from a look-alike of {supplier}’s domain, slipped into a genuine email thread.
Worse: someone set up a rule in the Accounts mailbox forwarding anything with ‘invoice’ in it to an outside address. They’ve been reading along.
Our mailboxes look clean. No odd sign-ins or forwarding rules so far.

beats.ask: Pick two things to do now.

options.text: Reset the Accounts team’s passwords and turn on multi-factor sign-in

variants.note: Not strictly needed this time, but a sensible precaution.

options.note: If they were in the mailbox, they had a password. Take it away and make sure they can’t use it again.

options.text: Check every mailbox for forwarding rules and remove any you find

variants.note: Nothing found this time, but always worth checking.

options.note: Forwarding rules are how attackers keep watching after you change the password.

options.text: Block the look-alike domain at the email gateway
options.note: Stops more fake emails from that domain reaching anyone.

options.text: Email the whole company about the scam right now
options.note: Useful later, but right now your people are better spent containing it, and the email system may not be trustworthy.

messages.text: How did {amount} just walk out of the door? I want whoever paid it dealt with.
So we nearly paid {amount} to criminals? I want to know whose mistake that was.

options.text: It’s a process gap: there was no call-back check. Fix the process and support the team
options.note: These emails are built to fool careful people. The missing control was the call-back, not a person.

reply.text: Fair. Make sure it can’t happen again.

options.text: First report it to Action Fraud and tell the insurer, then review what happened
options.note: Reporting quickly can help recovery, and insurers often require early notice.

reply.text: Reported. Insurer wants the timeline by Friday.

options.text: Agree, discipline the person who handled it
options.note: Blame teaches people to hide mistakes. Next time, nobody speaks up in time.

reply.text: I flagged it. I don’t understand why I’m in trouble.

options.text: Say nothing
options.note: Without a clear answer, the CEO draws their own conclusions.

reply.text: I’ll take that as ‘we don’t know’.

messages.text: The bank caught most of it before it moved on. We should get the bulk of {amount} back.

outcomes.note: Acting fast meant the bank could freeze most of the money.

messages.text: The bank says the money moved on within an hour. It’s gone.

outcomes.note: Without a quick call to the bank, the money was gone.

messages.text: Two of our other customers got the same email. Was it your system or ours that was breached?

options.text: Share what we’ve found (the fake domain, dates, how it reached us) and agree next steps
options.note: Working together finds the source faster and protects their other customers too.

reply.text: Thanks, that helps. We think one of our mailboxes was compromised. We’re on it.

options.text: Tell them it must have been their system
options.note: You don’t know yet, and blame damages a relationship you’ll need.

reply.text: That’s not helpful. We’ll be talking to our lawyers.

options.text: Say nothing until the lawyers are involved
options.note: Careful, but silence slows everyone down. You can share facts without admitting fault.

reply.text: Okay. We’ll wait to hear from you.

messages.text: The forwarding rule sent three weeks of Accounts email outside, including staff bank details from payroll queries. We found out yesterday.

beats.ask: Do we report it to the ICO?

options.text: Yes, report within 72 hours and tell the affected staff
options.note: Staff bank details are personal data. Report within 72 hours and tell the people affected so they can watch their accounts.

reply.text: Submitted, and I’m writing to the staff affected today.

options.text: Wait until we know exactly what was taken
options.note: The 72 hours started yesterday. Report what you know now and add details later.

reply.text: Okay, but we’re already a day in.

options.text: No need, it’s only internal email
options.note: It left the organisation, and it included bank details. That’s reportable.

reply.text: I don’t agree, and I’ll note that.

messages.text: No sign anyone got into our systems, so no personal data of ours has gone. The fake emails came entirely from outside.

beats.ask: What do we do about data protection?

options.text: Record the incident and our reasoning in the breach log
options.note: Even when nothing’s reportable, you record what happened and why you decided that.

reply.text: Logged.

options.text: Report it to the ICO anyway
options.note: Not needed here. Recording your reasoning is the key step.

reply.text: Sent. They may ask why.

options.text: Nothing to record
options.note: Security incidents should still be logged, even when no personal data was lost.

reply.text: We should still log it.

text: Now Harlow Office Supplies have emailed asking us to update their bank details too. It’s from their real domain and the same contact we’ve used for years.
Another one: Harlow Office Supplies want us to use a new bank account. Real email address, same person as always.

options.text: Call Harlow on the number we already hold before changing anything
options.note: It was genuine this time, and the call-back proved it. The same check works either way.

reply.text: Spoke to them. It’s real, they’ve moved banks. Updated.

options.text: Refuse all bank changes for a month
options.note: Safe, but it hurts genuine suppliers. A call-back keeps you safe without stopping the business.

reply.text: Harlow aren’t happy. Their payment will be late.

options.text: Process it, it’s from their real address
options.note: It was genuine this time, but real addresses get hijacked too, as you just saw. Always call back.

reply.text: Done. Fingers crossed.

messages.text: Right. What’s the one change that stops this happening again?

options.text: Make a call-back to a known number, plus a second person’s sign-off, mandatory for any bank change
options.note: This one control would have stopped the whole incident.

reply.text: In the finance manual from Monday.

options.text: Multi-factor sign-in on every mailbox
options.note: Stops attackers getting into mailboxes with stolen passwords. Pair it with the call-back rule.

reply.text: We’ll roll it out this month.

options.text: Fraud awareness training for the finance team
options.note: Helpful, but people under pressure still get fooled. A hard process check works every time.

reply.text: I’ll book a session.

options.text: Move to a different email provider
options.note: The provider wasn’t the problem. The missing check was.

reply.text: That’s a six-month project. Are we sure?

messages.text: We reported to the ICO after the 72 hours. They’ve asked for an explanation.

outcomes.note: The ICO report went in late.

messages.text: Jess has handed in her notice. The team’s nervous about raising anything now.

outcomes.note: Blaming an individual cost you a good person and made others less likely to speak up.

messages.text: The payment we sent after the warning is gone. The bank can’t recover it.

outcomes.note: Paying after doubts were raised lost the money.

messages.text: Good work, everyone. That could have been a lot worse.

outcomes.note: No nasty surprises afterwards.

scenarios.title: Supplier breach
scenarios.blurb: A supplier with access to your systems announces it’s been hacked. Are you next?

recap.text: The attackers **did use** {vendor}’s {tool} to get into your systems.
The attackers **never reached** your systems.
Your customers’ data **was** in what {vendor} lost.
None of your customers’ data **was** in what {vendor} lost.

text: {Vendor}, who run our {tool}, have just announced they’ve been hacked. Their statement says ‘some customers may be affected’.
It’s on the news: {vendor} have been breached. We use their {tool} on most of our servers.
Have you seen this? {Vendor} say attackers got into their systems over the weekend. They have access to ours through the {tool}.

options.text: Switch off {vendor}’s access to our systems until we know more
options.note: If a supplier is compromised, their access is the attacker’s access. Cut it first, restore it carefully later.

reply.text: Done. Their {tool} can’t reach us now. A few automated jobs will fail today.

options.text: Email {vendor} and wait for them to tell us what to do
options.note: They’re swamped and may not know yet. Protect yourself while you wait for answers.

reply.text: Auto-reply: ‘We’re experiencing high volumes. We’ll be in touch.’

options.text: Shut down every system {vendor} has ever touched
options.note: Safe, but cutting their access does almost the same job without stopping the business.

reply.text: Half the company can’t work. People are asking why.

options.text: Wait for more news before doing anything
options.note: Attackers move quickly once a supplier breach is public. Act on what you know.

reply.text: Okay. I’ll keep an eye on things.

messages.text: Found something: logins through {vendor}’s {tool} at 3am last night, using their account. That wasn’t them doing maintenance.
No logins through {vendor}’s {tool} since Friday afternoon. So far it looks like we weren’t touched.

beats.ask: Pick two jobs for the team.

options.text: Search our logs for everything their account did in the last 30 days
options.note: Find out what they touched before deciding what to clean.

options.text: Change every password and key {vendor} had for our systems
options.note: Whatever the attackers took from {vendor} stops working.

options.text: Preserve logs and copies of affected servers before changing anything
options.note: Evidence now is how you prove later what did, or didn’t, happen.

options.text: Tell all staff to change their own passwords
options.note: Not where the risk is. The supplier’s accounts are the way in.

messages.text: Our biggest client has seen the news. They want to know if their data is safe, or they’ll pause the contract.

options.text: What we know, what we don’t, what we’re doing, and when we’ll update them next
options.note: Honest and specific, with a time for the next update. Clients forgive incidents; they don’t forgive surprises.

reply.text: They appreciated that. They’ll wait for our update.

options.text: Reassure them that nothing of ours is affected

variants.note: You didn’t know that, and it wasn’t true. That promise will come back.

options.note: It turned out to be true, but you couldn’t know yet. Promise only what you know.

reply.text: They’re relieved. I hope we’re right.

options.text: Tell them it’s {vendor}’s problem, not ours
options.note: Your client chose you, and you chose the supplier. It’s your problem in their eyes.

reply.text: That didn’t land well.

options.text: Say nothing
options.note: Silence leaves the client imagining the worst.

reply.text: They’ve had no answer and they’re chasing me.

messages.text: Our contract says {vendor} must tell us about a breach within 24 hours. We heard about it from the news first.

options.text: Formally ask for their incident details and timeline, as the contract allows
options.note: Use the contract: you’re entitled to the facts you need for your own decisions and reports.

reply.text: Understood. Our incident lead will send you a full timeline by tomorrow morning.

options.text: Terminate the contract today
options.note: Satisfying, but you still need their help to investigate and you depend on them to run things.

reply.text: We can’t replace them overnight. Who’s running the {tool} now?

options.text: Leave them alone, they’re busy
options.note: You still need their facts to meet your own obligations.

reply.text: Then we’re making decisions without the facts.

messages.text: From the preserved logs: they made a hidden admin account at 3:12am. It’s removed, and we know exactly what they looked at.

outcomes.note: Preserved evidence showed exactly what the attackers did.

messages.text: They were in, but the logs from Monday morning have been overwritten. We can’t be sure what they touched.

outcomes.note: Without preserved logs, you can’t be sure what was touched.

messages.text: Confirmed: nothing came through {vendor}’s access. We were lucky, and quick.

outcomes.note: You confirmed you weren’t touched, rather than assuming it.

messages.text: {Vendor} have confirmed our customers’ names and email addresses were in the data they lost. We’re the controller; they’re our processor.

beats.ask: Who reports this to the ICO?

options.text: We do: report within 72 hours and warn customers about follow-up phishing
options.note: As the controller, reporting is your duty, even though the breach happened at your supplier.

reply.text: Submitted. The customer email goes out this afternoon.

options.text: {Vendor} should report it, it was their breach
options.note: The processor must tell you; you must tell the ICO. It’s your customers’ data.

reply.text: That’s not how controller and processor responsibilities work.

options.text: Wait for {vendor}’s full report first
options.note: Report what you know within 72 hours and add details later.

reply.text: Okay, but the clock’s running.

messages.text: {Vendor} have confirmed none of our customers’ data was in what they lost.

beats.ask: What do we do about data protection?

options.text: Record the incident and our reasoning in the breach log
options.note: Even when nothing’s reportable, you record what happened and why.

reply.text: Logged, with their confirmation attached.

options.text: Report it to the ICO anyway
options.note: Not needed here. Recording your reasoning is the key step.

reply.text: Sent.

options.text: Nothing to record
options.note: Security incidents should still be logged.

reply.text: We should still log it.

messages.text: Alert: another supplier, our backup company, has just pushed a software update to our servers.
There’s an update in their published release schedule for this week.

options.text: Check it against their published release notes and their status page before deciding
options.note: It was genuine. A quick check against what they’ve published is proportionate.

reply.text: Matches their release notes exactly. Letting it run.

options.text: Block all supplier updates for now
options.note: Cautious, but blocking every update leaves you missing security fixes too.

reply.text: Blocked. Their support team is asking why.

options.text: Let it run, it’s probably fine
options.note: It was fine this time, but today of all days, check first.

reply.text: Okay, letting it through.

messages.text: What do we change about how we work with suppliers?

options.text: Give suppliers only the access they need, only when they need it, with multi-factor sign-in
options.note: Limits what any one supplier breach can reach.

reply.text: We’ll switch them to on-request access this month.

options.text: Keep a register of every supplier with access, and review it twice a year
options.note: You can’t protect access you don’t know about.

reply.text: I’ll set it up.

options.text: Send every supplier a security questionnaire
options.note: Useful, but paperwork alone doesn’t limit what an attacker can reach.

reply.text: I’ll get it out.

options.text: Stop using outside suppliers altogether
options.note: Not realistic. Manage the risk rather than avoid every supplier.

reply.text: We couldn’t afford to do all that ourselves.

messages.text: Our ICO report went in after the 72 hours. They’ve asked why.

outcomes.note: The ICO report was late.

messages.text: The client found out we were affected after we told them we weren’t. They’ve paused the contract.

outcomes.note: Reassurance you couldn’t back up cost you the client’s trust.

messages.text: While we waited on Monday morning, they copied the HR folder using {vendor}’s access.

outcomes.note: Waiting gave the attackers time to take data.

messages.text: Good, calm work. Thank you.

outcomes.note: No nasty surprises afterwards.

scenarios.title: Insider leak
scenarios.blurb: Confidential files turn up somewhere they shouldn’t. Find out how, without making it worse.

recap.text: It was **deliberate**: a departing employee took the files.
It was an **accident**: a file shared with ‘anyone with the link’.
The files **included** staff personal data.
The files **didn’t include** personal data.

text: A client has just shown me {what}. It came from {where}. That should never have left this building.
We’ve got a leak. {What} turned up in {where}, and a client spotted it.
How has {what} ended up in {where}? I need answers today.

options.text: Quietly find out which files, who had access, and how they got out
options.note: Facts first, quietly. You don’t yet know if it was deliberate or an accident.

reply.text: On it. Pulling the access logs for that folder now.

options.text: Lock down the folder it came from
options.note: Stops any more getting out while you investigate.

reply.text: Locked. Only the leadership team can open it now.

options.text: Email the whole team: someone has leaked, and they will be found
options.note: It tips off whoever did it, and makes everyone else feel suspected.

reply.text: People are upset. Two have asked if they’re under suspicion.

options.text: Wait and see if anything else comes out
options.note: If it’s still leaking, every hour makes it worse.

reply.text: I’m not comfortable waiting.

messages.text: The logs show Jamie in Sales copied the whole folder to a USB stick on Friday. It’s his notice period; he’s joining a competitor next month.
The file was shared with ‘anyone with the link’ by mistake three weeks ago. It’s been opened 40 times from outside.

beats.ask: Pick two things to do now.

options.text: Remove the access or sharing link that let it out
options.note: Stops the leak at the source.

options.text: Preserve the logs and devices before anyone touches them
options.note: If this goes to HR or court, you’ll need the evidence intact.

options.text: Bring HR and legal in before speaking to anyone involved
options.note: People processes protect everyone, including the person involved.

options.text: Confront the person responsible straight away
options.note: Get the evidence and HR in place first. A confrontation can destroy both.

messages.text: Jamie’s still in the office until Friday. His manager wants to march him out in front of everyone.
The person who made the link has come forward. They’re mortified.

beats.ask: How do you handle the person involved?

options.text: Follow the proper HR process: fair, private, with the evidence

variants.note: Treat honest mistakes fairly, and people keep coming forward.

options.note: Suspend his access, interview him with HR, and keep it private. That protects you if it goes further.

reply.text: Arranged for this afternoon, in private.

options.text: Make an example of them in front of the team
options.note: Public shaming damages trust in leadership and can backfire legally.

reply.text: That’s gone round the whole office. People are rattled.

options.text: Do nothing about the person
options.note: Whether it was deliberate or not, there needs to be a proper, fair conversation.

reply.text: Okay, but people will ask what’s happening.

messages.text: The client wants to know how this happened, and whether their own information is safe with us.

beats.ask: What do we tell the client?

options.text: What happened, what we’ve done, and what we’re changing, without naming the individual
options.note: Open about the facts, careful about the person.

reply.text: They said they appreciate the straight answer.

options.text: Tell them exactly who did it
options.note: Naming an individual to a client can breach their rights and isn’t needed to reassure anyone.

reply.text: We really shouldn’t have named them.

options.text: Tell them it was nothing important
options.note: They’ve seen it. Minimising insults them.

reply.text: They didn’t buy that.

messages.text: The leaked files included staff salaries and home addresses. We found out yesterday.

beats.ask: Do we report it to the ICO?

options.text: Yes, within 72 hours, and tell the affected staff
options.note: Salaries and addresses are personal data. Report it and tell the people affected.

reply.text: Submitted. HR is talking to the staff affected today.

options.text: Wait until we know exactly who saw it
options.note: The 72 hours started yesterday. Report now; add details later.

reply.text: We’re already a day in.

options.text: No, it was only internal information
options.note: It left the organisation, and it’s personal data. That’s reportable.

reply.text: I disagree, and I’ll record that.

messages.text: No personal data in the leaked files, just commercial information.

beats.ask: What do we do about data protection?

options.text: Record the incident and our reasoning in the breach log
options.note: Record what happened and why it isn’t reportable.

reply.text: Logged.

options.text: Report it to the ICO anyway
options.note: Not needed. The ICO is about personal data.

reply.text: Sent, though it isn’t really theirs to deal with.

options.text: Nothing to record
options.note: Security incidents should still be logged.

reply.text: We should still log it.

messages.text: Legal say we could ask a court to stop the competitor using the material.

options.text: Yes, seek an injunction using the preserved evidence

variants.note: The right idea, but without preserved evidence the case is weak.

options.note: With the evidence intact, you can stop them using it.

reply.text: Filing today.

options.text: Publicly accuse the competitor on social media
options.note: It invites a defamation fight and drags your name through it.

reply.text: Their lawyers have been in touch.

options.text: Let it go; it’s out now
options.note: Sometimes reasonable, but they’ll keep using your material.

reply.text: I’m not happy, but fine.

messages.text: Should we change how file sharing works for everyone?

options.text: Turn off ‘anyone with the link’ sharing; share with named people only
options.note: Removes the setting that caused the leak, without stopping people working.

reply.text: Changed tonight.

options.text: Turn off all sharing outside the company
options.note: Safe, but people need to share with clients. They’ll find riskier workarounds.

reply.text: Done. Sales are already complaining.

options.text: Leave it as it is
options.note: The same mistake will happen again.

reply.text: Okay.

messages.text: Alert: Priya in Finance has just emailed a large spreadsheet to an outside address.
That’ll be the year-end pack for our auditors. It’s due today.

beats.ask: How do you handle the alert?

options.text: Confirm with Priya that it went to the auditors’ known address
options.note: It was genuine. A quick check is proportionate, even straight after a leak.

reply.text: Yes, their usual address. All fine.

options.text: Block it and suspend Priya’s account
options.note: After a leak it’s tempting, but she was doing her job. Check first.

reply.text: The auditors are waiting and Priya’s locked out.

options.text: Ignore it
options.note: Fine this time, but alerts like this are exactly what would catch the next leak.

reply.text: Noted, not checked.

messages.text: What’s the one change that stops this happening again?

options.text: Alerts on unusual bulk downloads and public sharing links
options.note: Catches both the deliberate and the accidental kind, early.

reply.text: We’ll switch those alerts on this month.

options.text: When someone hands in their notice, review and reduce their access straight away
options.note: Leavers are the highest-risk group for deliberate leaks.

reply.text: Adding it to the leavers checklist.

options.text: Ban USB sticks and personal email completely
options.note: Helps a bit, but determined people find other ways and honest ones are slowed down.

reply.text: We can do that, but expect complaints.

options.text: Monitor everyone’s screens
options.note: Disproportionate, damaging to trust, and likely unlawful without strong justification.

reply.text: We’d need a very strong reason for that, and we don’t have one.

messages.text: Our ICO report went in after the 72 hours. They’ve asked why.

outcomes.note: The ICO report was late.

messages.text: Morale’s low. People feel blamed for something most of them had nothing to do with.

outcomes.note: Public blame hurt the whole team’s trust.

messages.text: Without preserved evidence, we can’t prove what Jamie took.

outcomes.note: Unpreserved evidence weakened your position.

messages.text: Handled fairly and properly. Thank you.

outcomes.note: No nasty surprises afterwards.

scenarios.title: Open cloud storage
scenarios.blurb: A researcher finds your customer files open to the internet. Close it, find out who looked, and do right by everyone.

recap.text: Strangers **did download** the files before it was closed.
Nobody **but the researcher** downloaded anything.
With access logging off, you **couldn’t tell** who had looked.
It had been open for **{days}**.

text: Hi, I found a cloud storage bucket belonging to {org} that’s open to the internet. It holds {data}. I only downloaded a small sample to confirm. Please fix it soon.
Security researcher here. Your storage at {org} is publicly readable, including {data}. I’ve not shared anything. Can someone fix it?
Reporting a problem responsibly: anyone can read {org}’s cloud bucket containing {data}. Happy to help confirm the fix.

beats.ask: It’s Saturday morning. What do you do?

options.text: Log in to our own cloud console and make the storage private now
options.note: Close it first, from your own console (never from a link in the email), then investigate.

reply.text: Done. It’s private now. I checked from outside: access denied.

options.text: Delete everything in it straight away
options.note: It closes the leak, but destroys the evidence of what was exposed, and maybe data you need.

reply.text: Deleted. Hope we didn’t need any of it.

options.text: Ignore it, it could be a scam
options.note: Check it safely yourself, in your own console. Ignoring it leaves it open.

reply.text: Following up: it’s still open.

options.text: Leave it until the team’s in on Monday
options.note: Once someone’s found it, others can too. Weekends don’t pause attackers.

reply.text: Okay, I’ll look first thing Monday.

messages.text: It’s been open for {days}, left over from a test project.
Good news: access logging was switched on, so we can see who downloaded what.
Bad news: access logging was off. We can’t see who downloaded anything.

beats.ask: Pick two things to do now.

options.text: Go through the access logs for downloads from unknown addresses

variants.note: Logging was off, so there were no logs to check. A wasted pair of hands.

options.note: The logs tell you whether this is a near miss or a breach.

options.text: Check all our other cloud storage for the same mistake
options.note: Where there’s one, there’s often another.

options.text: Change any passwords or keys that were stored in the files
options.note: Anything secret in there has to be treated as known.

options.text: Reply to thank the researcher and ask exactly what they saw
options.note: They’re helping you. Treat them as an ally.

messages.text: Thanks for fixing it so quickly. I’d like to publish a short write-up in 30 days, without naming you if you prefer. Is that okay?

options.text: Thank them, agree a date, and keep them updated
options.note: Responsible disclosure works both ways. A good relationship turns a risk into a story about doing the right thing.

reply.text: Brilliant, thank you. I’ll send you a draft first.

options.text: Threaten legal action if they publish anything
options.note: Threatening someone who reported responsibly is how small incidents become headlines.

reply.text: That’s disappointing. I’ll take advice.

options.text: Offer them money to stay quiet
options.note: Paying for silence looks like a cover-up, and doesn’t change your legal duties.

reply.text: I’m not asking for money. I just want it fixed and to share the lesson.

messages.text: The logs show two unknown addresses downloaded the whole bucket last month. This is a real breach.

outcomes.note: The logs confirmed strangers took the files. Painful, but now you know.

messages.text: We’ve found the files for sale on a forum. With no logs, we can’t say who took them or when.

outcomes.note: Without logs, you only found out because the files turned up for sale.

messages.text: Only one download in the logs: the researcher’s small sample. Nobody else touched it.

outcomes.note: Logging turned a frightening weekend into a near miss.

messages.text: No sign of the files anywhere, but with logging off we can’t rule out that someone took them.

outcomes.note: Without logs, you can’t prove nobody looked.

messages.text: Customers’ {data} were taken. We became aware on Saturday.

options.text: Report to the ICO within 72 hours and tell the affected customers what to watch for
options.note: A confirmed breach of customer data: report it, and help the people affected protect themselves.

reply.text: Report in. Customer emails go out today.

options.text: Wait until we know exactly which customers
options.note: The 72 hours started on Saturday. Report now; add detail later.

reply.text: We’re two days in already.

options.text: Don’t report; it was a cloud setting, not a hack
options.note: How it happened doesn’t matter. Personal data was exposed and taken.

reply.text: That’s not how it works, and I’ll record my objection.

messages.text: We can’t prove nobody downloaded the {data}. We’ve known since Saturday.

options.text: Report to the ICO within 72 hours, explaining we can’t rule out access
options.note: When you can’t rule out that personal data was seen, treat it as a breach and report it.

reply.text: Report in, with our reasoning.

options.text: Assume nobody saw it and move on
options.note: ‘We don’t know’ isn’t the same as ‘it didn’t happen’.

reply.text: I don’t think we can assume that.

options.text: Wait a week to see if anything turns up
options.note: The 72 hours started on Saturday.

reply.text: The deadline won’t wait a week.

messages.text: The logs show only the researcher’s sample was downloaded.

options.text: Record it in the breach log with the evidence, and our decision not to report
options.note: With logs proving no wider access, recording your reasoning is the right step.

reply.text: Logged, with the access logs attached.

options.text: Report it to the ICO anyway
options.note: Cautious and not harmful, but the evidence shows it wasn’t needed.

reply.text: Sent.

options.text: No need to record anything, no harm done
options.note: It was still a breach of security. Record it.

reply.text: We still need to record it.

messages.text: Our new scan has flagged another public storage bucket.
That one holds the images on our public website.

options.text: Check it only holds website images, then mark it as public on purpose
options.note: Some storage is meant to be public. Confirm it, record it, move on.

reply.text: Just images. Marked as intentionally public.

options.text: Lock it down like the other one
options.note: Cautious, but the website’s images just disappeared.

reply.text: The website’s lost all its pictures.

options.text: Ignore the alert
options.note: It was fine, but you couldn’t know that without looking.

reply.text: Okay, leaving it.

messages.text: How do we make sure this never happens again?

options.text: Block public access by default on all cloud storage, with a sign-off for exceptions
options.note: Make the safe setting the default, so a mistake needs effort.

reply.text: We can enforce that across the whole account.

options.text: Turn on access logging for everything
options.note: Next time, you’ll know straight away who looked.

reply.text: Switching it on today.

options.text: Remind staff to be careful with cloud settings
options.note: A reminder helps a little. A safe default helps a lot more.

reply.text: I’ll send something round.

options.text: Stop using cloud storage
options.note: Not realistic, and the problem was a setting, not the cloud.

reply.text: Half our systems run there.

messages.text: Our ICO report went in after the 72 hours. They’ve asked why.

outcomes.note: The ICO report was late.

messages.text: The researcher has posted about our legal threat. It’s getting a lot of attention.

outcomes.note: Threatening the researcher became the story.

messages.text: Because the files were deleted, we can’t tell customers exactly what was exposed.

outcomes.note: Deleting the data destroyed evidence you needed.

messages.text: Another download happened on Sunday, while it was still open.

outcomes.note: Waiting until Monday let another copy walk out.

messages.text: Quick, honest and thorough. Thank you.

outcomes.note: No nasty surprises afterwards.

scenarios.title: Launch-day DDoS
scenarios.blurb: Your biggest launch of the year, and the site is buckling under fake traffic.

recap.text: The attackers **demanded a ransom** to stop.
There was **no ransom demand**, just disruption.
The flood was **cover** for a break-in on the staff email server.
It was **just a flood**. Nothing else was attacked.

text: {Product} went live at 8. Traffic is {peak} normal and the site is falling over. It doesn’t look like real customers.
We’re being flooded. {Peak} our usual traffic, all from strange places, and {product} keeps timing out.
Something’s very wrong with the launch. Traffic is {peak} normal and almost none of it is real people.

options.text: Call our hosting provider and switch on their DDoS protection
options.note: Large floods are best absorbed upstream, by people built for it.

reply.text: Protection’s on. We’re filtering the bad traffic now. Give it ten minutes.

options.text: Add more servers to soak it up
options.note: It helps a bit, but it’s expensive and the attackers can usually send more than you can add.

reply.text: More servers are up. They’re being flooded too.

options.text: Take the site offline until it stops
options.note: That’s doing the attackers’ job for them. Filter the flood instead.

reply.text: Site’s down. Launch day, and nobody can buy anything.

options.text: Wait, it might be genuine demand
options.note: Your team’s telling you it isn’t real customers. Act on it.

reply.text: It’s getting worse.

messages.text: We’ve had an email: ‘Pay 5 bitcoin and the attack stops. Price doubles every hour.’

options.text: Don’t pay. Report it to Action Fraud and keep the evidence
options.note: Paying marks you as a payer and funds the next attack. Report it and keep defending.

reply.text: Reported, and I’ve saved the email.

options.text: Pay, it’s launch day
options.note: There’s no guarantee they’ll stop, and they’ll be back for more.

reply.text: Paid. The traffic hasn’t dropped.

options.text: Reply to negotiate the price down
options.note: Engaging tells them you’re willing. Don’t.

reply.text: They’ve replied: the price just went up.

options.text: Leave it
options.note: Not paying was right, but report it and keep the evidence.

reply.text: No reply sent. What should I do with the email?

messages.text: Customers are angry on social media, and two journalists are asking why the launch has failed.

options.text: Our site is under a deliberate attack; we’re dealing with it. Updates on our status page.
options.note: Honest and simple. Customers are far more forgiving of an attack than of being misled.

reply.text: Posted. Lots of supportive replies.

options.text: Say it’s down to huge demand for the launch
options.note: Spinning an attack as ‘demand’ tends to unravel, and then you look dishonest.

reply.text: A journalist has asked why ‘demand’ is coming from thousands of hijacked devices.

options.text: Say nothing until it’s fixed
options.note: Silence on launch day makes people assume the worst.

reply.text: People are now asking if we’ve been hacked and are hiding it.

messages.text: While everyone’s watching the website, I’ve spotted unusual admin sign-ins on the staff email server.
Nothing unusual anywhere else on the network so far.

beats.ask: Where does the security team put its attention?

options.text: Split the team: keep people watching everything else, not just the website

variants.note: Exactly right. The flood was a distraction, and you caught the real break-in.

options.note: Floods are sometimes cover for something quieter. Keep watching everything.

reply.text: Two of us are on the email server and the rest of the network.

options.text: Everyone on the website until it’s fixed

variants.note: That’s what the attackers wanted. The break-in went unwatched.

options.note: Nothing else was happening this time, but keep some eyes elsewhere.

reply.text: Everyone’s on the site.

options.text: Turn off other alerts so the team isn’t distracted
options.note: Turning off alerts during an attack blinds you to whatever else is going on.

reply.text: Other alerts muted.

messages.text: We’ve got paid adverts running all day. Do we carry on?

options.text: Pause the adverts until the site’s stable, then restart them
options.note: No point paying to send people to a broken site.

reply.text: Paused. We’ll restart once things are steady.

options.text: Keep them running, it’s launch day
options.note: You’re paying to send customers to a site that won’t load.

reply.text: Running. Most clicks are bouncing.

options.text: Cancel the whole launch
options.note: An overreaction. The flood is being filtered; delay, don’t cancel.

reply.text: That’s months of work thrown away.

messages.text: Another huge traffic spike!
Our TV advert has just gone out.

options.text: Check the traffic pattern: real phones, from the UK, buying things?
options.note: It was real customers after the advert. A quick look told you not to block them.

reply.text: Real customers, and they’re buying. Brilliant.

options.text: Block it, it’s the attack again
options.note: You just blocked your real customers on launch night.

reply.text: Sales have dropped to zero.

options.text: Ignore it
options.note: Fine this time, but a quick check tells you whether to act.

reply.text: It’s holding up.

messages.text: The attack’s dropped off and our filtering’s holding. Do you want to keep the protection on?

options.text: Keep it on, and review the attack with the provider tomorrow
options.note: Attackers often come back once they think you’ve relaxed.

reply.text: Leaving it on. Review booked for 10am.

options.text: Turn it off to save money
options.note: It’s rarely over after one day.

reply.text: Switched off.

options.text: Keep basic protection but turn off the expensive extras
options.note: A reasonable middle ground, but wait until you’re sure it’s over.

reply.text: Done.

messages.text: What do we do differently for the next big launch?

options.text: Always-on DDoS protection, and a tested plan before every big launch
options.note: Big launches are predictable targets. Be ready before the day.

reply.text: We’ll run a test together before the next one.

options.text: A status page and pre-written messages ready to go
options.note: When things go wrong, the first hour of communication matters most.

reply.text: I’ll have them drafted by Friday.

options.text: Load-test the site before launches
options.note: Good practice for real demand, but it doesn’t stop a deliberate flood.

reply.text: Adding it to the launch checklist.

options.text: Keep launch dates secret next time
options.note: You need customers to know about your launch. Prepare instead.

reply.text: That rather defeats the point of a launch.

messages.text: They came back the next morning, and with the protection off we were down for three hours.

outcomes.note: Switching protection off too soon let them back in.

messages.text: The same group attacked again on Friday and asked for twice as much.

outcomes.note: Paying marked you as a target.

messages.text: We’ve found the email server break-in from launch day. They’d been reading leadership email for a week.

outcomes.note: With everyone on the website, the real break-in went unnoticed.

messages.text: Not the launch we planned, but well handled.

outcomes.note: No nasty surprises afterwards.
